items.name: Sarah Ahmed
items.quote: The daily plan honestly saved me from going in circles. I open the platform knowing exactly what to do — no more guessing.

items.name: Omar Khaled
items.quote: The mock exams made the biggest difference. I walked into the real test feeling like I'd done it before — same atmosphere, exactly.

items.name: Noura Saad
items.quote: The best part is the assessment after every test. It shows you exactly where your weak points are, instead of wasting time redoing the whole syllabus.

items.question: How does Khatwa build my study plan?
items.answer: After the placement test, the system analyzes your results in every skill area and factors in your goal and available study hours, then builds a daily plan spread across 40, 60, or 90 days.

items.question: How closely do the mock exams match the real STEP exam?
items.answer: Each mock exam follows the same structure and timing as the real STEP: 100 questions in 150 minutes, split between reading, grammar, listening, and writing analysis — so you know what to expect on test day.

items.question: Do I need a subscription to get started?
items.answer: No — you can create a free account, take the placement test, and start on the basic plan right away. Pro and Premium plans unlock additional content and features.

items.question: Can I use the platform from my phone?
items.answer: The platform is fully responsive on every device, and works as a web app you can install on your phone's home screen.

aboutPage.title: About Khatwa
aboutPage.body: Khatwa is a smart study platform built for students preparing for the STEP exam in Saudi Arabia. It combines a placement test, a personalized study plan, realistic mock exams, vocabulary tools, and clear analytics — so you always know what to study next.
aboutPage.body2: Our goal is simple: make high-quality STEP preparation accessible to every student, with a calm experience that keeps you focused on raising your score.

contactPage.title: Contact us
contactPage.body: Have a question or feedback? We'd love to hear from you.

privacyPage.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPage.body: We collect only the information needed to provide the service — such as your name and email address when you create an account.
privacyPage.body2: Your data is used to personalize your study plan, track your progress, and improve the platform. We never sell your personal information.
privacyPage.body3: You can request a copy or deletion of your data at any time from your settings page.

termsPage.title: Terms of Service
termsPage.body: By creating an account, you agree to use Khatwa for personal, non-commercial study purposes only.
termsPage.body2: Content on the platform is provided for educational purposes and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the official STEP exam body.
termsPage.body3: We may update these terms from time to time. Continued use of the platform after changes means you accept the updated terms.

course-vocabulary.title: Vocabulary Building

course-tips.title: General Exam Tips
course-tips.description: Small habits that raise your score without extra studying.

course-strategies.title: Time Management on the Exam

course-revision.title: Comprehensive Review
course-revision.description: Reinforce what you learned this week with questions from all sections.

lesson-grammar-1.title: Subject-Verb Agreement and Tenses
lesson-grammar-1.notes: The key rule: the verb agrees with the subject in number, not with the nearest noun in the sentence. Phrases like "Neither of", "Each of", and "The number of" are always treated as singular subjects. As for tenses, the past perfect (had + past participle) describes an event that happened before another past event mentioned in the sentence.

lesson-reading-1.title: Reading for Main Ideas and Details
lesson-reading-1.notes: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph first to get a general sense of the topic before reading the details. When answering a detail question, look for the question's keywords inside the text rather than relying on memory.

lesson-listening-1.title: Following Short Conversations
lesson-listening-1.notes: In listening conversations, the second speaker often gives a correction or an important detail after "No" or "Actually". Pay attention to these words because they often signal information that will be tested.

lesson-writingAnalysis-1.title: Spotting Grammar Errors Quickly
lesson-writingAnalysis-1.notes: Start by checking subject-verb agreement first, as it is the most common error. Then check prepositions, and finally dangling modifiers — opening phrases that don't describe the right subject.

lesson-vocabulary-1.title: Spaced Repetition for Vocabulary
lesson-vocabulary-1.notes: Reviewing a new word after one day, then after 3 days, then after a week locks it into long-term memory better than reviewing it 10 times in a single day. Use the vocabulary section on the platform to track this automatically.

lesson-tips-1.title: Small Habits, Big Difference
lesson-tips-1.notes: Read all four options before choosing your answer, even if the first one seems correct. Flag the questions you're unsure about and come back to them after finishing, since time pressure eases after answering the easier questions first.

lesson-strategies-1.title: Spreading 150 Minutes Across 100 Questions
lesson-strategies-1.notes: Allocate approximate time per section based on its number of questions: reading and grammar need more time per question than listening. Don't spend more than a minute and a half per grammar or written-analysis question on average.

lesson-revision-1.title: Comprehensive Weekly Review
lesson-revision-1.notes: Selected questions from all sections to review what you learned this week.

lesson-grammar-2.title: Passive Voice and Deduction with Modal Verbs
lesson-grammar-2.notes: The passive voice is used when the subject is unknown or unimportant: "will be announced", not "will announce". As for modals, "must" signals a strong logical deduction based on available evidence, while "might" signals a weaker possibility. In reported speech, "will" shifts back to "would" when the reporting verb is in the past.

lesson-reading-2.title: Extracting Implicit and Explicit Information
lesson-reading-2.notes: Some questions ask for explicit information stated literally in the text (ask yourself: where exactly is this sentence?), while others require inference (ask yourself: what is the writer hinting at without saying directly?). Distinguish between the two before choosing your answer.

lesson-listening-2.title: Conversations in Formal Contexts
lesson-listening-2.notes: In formal conversations (bookings, academic consultations), pay attention to numerical details (time, number) because they are often the focus of the question, and also to the reason the speaker gives for preferring one option over another.

lesson-writingAnalysis-2.title: Parallelism and Pronoun Case Errors
lesson-writingAnalysis-2.notes: When a list of verbs is joined with "and", they must all be in the same grammatical form (parallel structure). Remember that subject pronouns (I, he, she) are not used after prepositions like "between"; object pronouns (me, him, her) are used instead.

lesson-vocabulary-2.title: Common Academic Vocabulary in Reading
lesson-vocabulary-2.notes: Words like infrastructure, curriculum, and sustained appear frequently in academic reading texts. Memorize them within a full sentence rather than as a single word — this locks them into memory better and helps you recognize them in different contexts.

lesson-tips-2.title: The Day Before the Exam
lesson-tips-2.notes: Avoid studying new material on the last day; instead focus on reviewing the recurring mistakes in your previous tests. Confirm the exam location and time in advance, and get enough sleep — fatigue affects reading speed and attention more than most students realize.

lesson-strategies-2.title: When to Skip a Difficult Question
lesson-strategies-2.notes: If a question takes more than two minutes without progress, flag it and move on instead of losing time that could go to easier questions. Return to deferred questions during the final review, when you'll often see them with a clearer perspective.

lesson-revision-2.title: Weekly Review 2
lesson-revision-2.notes: A second round of selected questions from all sections to reinforce what you learned.

lesson-grammar-3.title: Advanced Structures: Causatives, Inversion, and Noun Clauses
lesson-grammar-3.notes: The causative "have something done" is used when someone else performs the action for you, with the verb in past participle form: "have my car repaired". Inversion happens after negative adverbs like "Rarely" at the start of a sentence: "Rarely do we see...". Remember that "whether" can begin a noun clause in subject position, unlike "if".

lesson-reading-3.title: Reading Opinion and Argumentative Texts
lesson-reading-3.notes: In argumentative texts (like the debate over standardized testing), always look for both sides' views: the proponents and the opponents, because questions often test your ability to tell one side's argument apart from the other's.

lesson-listening-3.title: Conversations in Hotels and Universities
lesson-listening-3.notes: In service conversations (hotels, bookings, academic appointments), pay attention to the final solution the second speaker proposes after an apology or clarification — it is often the focus of the main question.

lesson-writingAnalysis-3.title: Comma, Possessive, and Double-Negative Errors
lesson-writingAnalysis-3.notes: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma and no conjunction is called a "comma splice" and is a common mistake. Remember that the possessive of a singular noun adds 's, not s' alone. As for double negatives like "don't have no", they should be corrected to "don't have any".

lesson-vocabulary-3.title: Vocabulary from New Reading Texts
lesson-vocabulary-3.notes: Words like benchmark, arable, and entrepreneur recur in modern academic reading texts about education, technology, and urban farming. Review them in context in the vocabulary section for better retention.

lesson-tips-3.title: Exam Day: Final Tips
lesson-tips-3.notes: Read the full instructions before starting each section even if they feel familiar, since some exams introduce slight changes to the instructions. Keep breathing calmly if you feel nervous — excessive anxiety slows reading speed more than anything else.

lesson-strategies-3.title: Dealing with Anxiety During the Exam
lesson-strategies-3.notes: If you feel anxious in the middle of the exam, stop for just five seconds and take a deep breath instead of continuing to read without comprehension. Reminding yourself that you've studied these same patterns before reduces stress and brings back focus quickly.

lesson-revision-3.title: Weekly Review 3
lesson-revision-3.notes: A third round of selected questions from all sections, focusing on the newest structures and vocabulary.

lesson-grammar-4.title: Advanced Conditionals and Inversion
lesson-grammar-4.notes: When a conditional starts with Had instead of If (Had I known), If is dropped and the sentence is inverted. Adverbs like "No sooner...than" and "Only after..." force inversion too, moving the auxiliary before the subject.

lesson-reading-4.title: Reading Environmental Texts
lesson-reading-4.notes: Environmental texts appear often in the exam: ocean pollution, microplastics, recycling. Focus on cause and effect between sentences, because questions usually ask "why" or "what do researchers suggest", which are usually answered by one sentence in the middle of the passage.

lesson-listening-4.title: Memberships and Promotional Offers
lesson-listening-4.notes: In membership conversations (gyms, services), pay attention to what the more expensive plan adds over the basic one, and why the speaker chooses in the end — the reason is often a price or a feature mentioned only once.

lesson-writingAnalysis-4.title: Comma Splices
lesson-writingAnalysis-4.notes: When you see two complete sentences joined by only a comma with no conjunction (a comma splice), that is the error. The correct fix is either to separate the two sentences or to add a connector like "because" or "and".

lesson-vocabulary-4.title: Vocabulary from Environmental and Science Texts
lesson-vocabulary-4.notes: Words like decompose, ingest, microplastic, and compound appear constantly in environmental texts. Link each word to the context it appears in (plastic decomposes, animals ingest) instead of memorizing it in isolation.

lesson-grammar-5.title: Correlative Comparatives and so/such
lesson-grammar-5.notes: The structure "The + comparative, the + comparative" expresses a proportional relationship (The more you practice, the better you become). Meanwhile "So + adjective + that" expresses a result: (so long that).

lesson-reading-5.title: Inference from Scientific Texts
lesson-reading-5.notes: Inference questions do not find their answer literally in the text; you derive it from the sum of the sentences. Read the final sentence of the paragraph carefully, because many inferences are built on the writer's concluding statement.

lesson-listening-5.title: Purchases and Returns
lesson-listening-5.notes: In purchase and return conversations, listen for the type of resolution the speaker chooses at the end (cash refund, exchange, store credit). Hearing a seller question like "Do you have the receipt?" signals a condition in the return policy.

lesson-writingAnalysis-5.title: Confusable Words: affect/effect and amount/number
lesson-writingAnalysis-5.notes: Distinguish between affect (verb: to influence) and effect (noun: result). Also use amount for uncountable nouns and number for countable ones. These errors appear deliberately in questions to trap those who confuse them.

lesson-vocabulary-5.title: Everyday Listening Vocabulary
lesson-vocabulary-5.notes: Listening conversations revolve around memberships, appointments, and airports. Memorize practical terms like membership, exchange, connecting flight, and boarding pass, and link each to the scenario you hear it in.

lesson-grammar-6.title: Passive Voice Across Tenses
lesson-grammar-6.notes: The passive voice is always: the right tense of "be" + the past participle. Future: will be published, past: was published. First check who performs the action: if no doer is mentioned, the sentence is usually passive.

lesson-reading-6.title: Health and Behavior Texts
lesson-reading-6.notes: Health and behavior texts (sleep, habits, focus) usually present a general concept and then support it with study findings. Distinguish between the theoretical concept and the practical finding, since a question may ask for either.

lesson-listening-6.title: Travel and Flight Delays
lesson-listening-6.notes: In travel conversations, track three details: the reason for the delay, the solution the agent offers, and how the passenger will receive the new information (email, message). These three are usually the focus of the questions.

lesson-writingAnalysis-6.title: Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement
lesson-writingAnalysis-6.notes: Words like Each, Everyone, and Anybody are grammatically singular, so they must be followed by a singular pronoun (his or her). Always check the subject before judging the pronoun in the sentence.

lesson-vocabulary-6.title: Synonyms That Raise Your Score
lesson-vocabulary-6.notes: Synonyms give you flexibility in reading and writing: consolidate instead of strengthen, compound instead of accumulate, ingest instead of swallow. Every synonym you add expands your understanding of new texts.

lesson-grammar-7.title: Noun Clauses and the Verb After Suggestions
lesson-grammar-7.notes: After verbs like suggest and recommend with that, the verb comes in its bare infinitive form: suggest that the report be submitted. Also remember that some verbs require an -ing form after a preposition, such as object to having.

lesson-reading-7.title: Public Services and Community Texts
lesson-reading-7.notes: Public services texts (libraries, transport, facilities) usually compare past and present, or present a financial challenge. Look for the community that benefits most, and the main threat — these are two recurring questions.

lesson-listening-7.title: Formal Calls and Interviews
lesson-listening-7.notes: In formal calls (HR, work appointments), listen for the proposed time first, then what the speaker does after the call (sends an email, confirms attendance). The order of events is the key to the correct answer.

lesson-writingAnalysis-7.title: Dangling Modifiers and Parallelism
lesson-writingAnalysis-7.notes: An opening phrase like Walking down the street must describe the subject that follows it immediately. If it doesn't, it dangles. And when multiple verbs appear in a single list, keep their forms perfectly parallel.

lesson-vocabulary-7.title: Understanding Words from Context
lesson-vocabulary-7.notes: Don't reach for the dictionary for every new word; guess first from the surrounding sentences. The sentence after a strange word often explains or contrasts it, which builds faster reading skill.

lesson-grammar-8.title: Correlative Conjunctions and Parallelism
lesson-grammar-8.notes: Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs: not only...but also, neither...nor. When a list of verbs or nouns appears, keep the same form across all items (parallelism) — this is key to succeeding in both grammar and writing questions.

lesson-reading-8.title: Identifying the Writer's Opinion
lesson-reading-8.notes: To identify the writer's opinion, look for evaluative phrases: more valuable, counterproductive, critical. When a text presents an argument and weakens the opposing side, that is a clear signal of the writer's position.

lesson-listening-8.title: Extracting Precise Details
lesson-listening-8.notes: Some listening questions ask about a small detail mentioned only once: a number, a condition (like showing a receipt), or a location. Listen to the second half of the employee's or seller's answer, since it often contains the required condition or detail.

lesson-writingAnalysis-8.title: Collective Nouns and Agreement
lesson-writingAnalysis-8.notes: A collective noun (team, committee) is singular in connected meaning, and phrases like "as well as" or "along with" do not make the subject plural. Also watch the relative clause who: its verb follows its immediate antecedent (one of the students who have).

lesson-vocabulary-8.title: Final Vocabulary Review
lesson-vocabulary-8.notes: Review your oldest cards before the newer ones, because forgotten words need more reinforcement than recent ones. Set aside 10 minutes daily for spaced-repetition review in the vocabulary section before your mock exam.
